narrative:
The 2020 Houston Astros played their abbreviated 60-game season under a cloud — ostracized by the rest of baseball following the sign-stealing scandal revelations, they took the field without fans, without sympathy, and without the benefit of the doubt. Yet they were still a talented team, and for much of the summer they competed hard enough to remind observers why they had been so dangerous in the first place. A 4-3 July gave way to a genuinely strong August (15-11), built on the kind of clutch home run production that had always defined their best baseball — George Springer going deep with a runner on in a walk-off moment, Alex Bregman launching a two-run shot, Kyle Tucker beginning to emerge as a legitimate force.

September was where the season unraveled. Going 10-17 in the final month, the Astros were battered by a bullpen that couldn't hold leads and a rotation that began to crack under the accumulated pressure of a short, strange season. Ryan Pressly, one of their most trusted relievers, appeared repeatedly in the wrong column — surrendering key doubles and a crushing homer as games slipped away. The Angels torched them on a single brutal September night, with Anthony Rendon's three-run blast off rookie Humberto Castellanos serving as the defining image of a team in freefall. They stumbled into October more than they marched.

Still, the postseason offered a reset. A wild card win over Minnesota and a division series victory over Oakland — where Altuve delivered in the clutch as he always seemed to — pushed the Astros into the ALCS against the Tampa Bay Rays. There, the magic ran thin. A lineup built for power and experience struggled against Tampa's pitching and the electric Randy Arozarena, and the bullpen — Josh James in particular — continued to hemorrhage runs at the worst moments. Carlos Correa's home run in Game 4 offered a flash of the old Houston swagger, but it wasn't enough to reverse the tide.

The 2020 Astros were a team caught between two identities: the dynasty that had defined the late 2010s and the rebuilding club that would eventually re-emerge on the other side of controversy. They were good enough to reach the final four, but not good enough — or perhaps not whole enough — to go any further. It was a season that ended, like so many things in 2020, with a sense of incompletion.

chapters.title: Pariah Summer
chapters.description: A rocky opening stretch defined by early bullpen misfires sets the tone for a team playing under a harsh spotlight.

chapters.title: August Surge
chapters.description: Springer, Bregman, and Tucker power a strong 15-11 August that proves this lineup still has serious firepower.

chapters.title: September Slide
chapters.description: A 10-17 September exposes a shaky bullpen and rotation as the Astros stumble toward the playoff cutoff.

chapters.title: Wild Card and Onward
chapters.description: The Astros survive October's opening rounds on clutch hits and veteran composure to reach the ALCS.

chapters.title: Rays End the Run
chapters.description: Tampa Bay's pitching and the brilliance of Randy Arozarena extinguish Houston's postseason hopes in the ALCS.
